papers.title: The Transformer Cookbook
papers.authors: Andy Yang, Christopher Watson, Anton Xue, Satwik Bhattamishra, Jose Llarena, William Merrill, Emile Dos Santos Ferreira, Anej Svete, and David Chiang
papers.standfirst: A collection of recipes for turning algorithms into transformer weights.
intro: This example post shows how a highlight can grow out of its recommendations. The sample readers below are drawn to the prospect of sharing constructions and helping more people start working with them.
Their comments are the main story here. An author-written guide or short video can sit alongside them if the authors choose to contribute.

endorsements.name: Example reader A
endorsements.text: What excites me is the possibility of making constructive arguments much easier to share. I can imagine using this as a common reference in a reading group, so we spend less time reconstructing the machinery and more time asking new questions.

endorsements.name: Example reader B
endorsements.text: I would recommend this to someone who wants to move from understanding a transformer argument to trying a construction of their own. That change in confidence is why I think it deserves attention.

endorsements.name: Example reader C
endorsements.text: This feels like the kind of resource I would keep returning to when starting a new project.

authorGuide.title: A short route into the paper
paragraphs: Start with one construction and follow it from the problem statement to the finished model. Work through a small example before moving on to the general recipe.
A useful reading-group exercise is to adapt the construction to a nearby problem, then compare which parts carry over.

papers.title: What Formal Languages Can Transformers Express? A Survey
papers.authors: Lena Strobl, William Merrill, Gail Weiss, David Chiang, and Dana Angluin
papers.standfirst: A map of expressivity results—and the assumptions that make them fit together.
intro: This example brings together two imagined reasons for recommending a survey: connecting results and making the area easier to enter. A real post would quote the actual public recommendations.

endorsements.name: Example reader A
endorsements.text: The implication I care about is a more productive conversation across results. Having a shared map could help us notice when we disagree about assumptions rather than about what a model can do.

endorsements.name: Example reader B
endorsements.text: I would put this on a reading-group list because it could give newcomers a way to join discussions that otherwise assume a lot of background.

papers.title: Thinking Like Transformers
papers.authors: Gail Weiss, Yoav Goldberg, and Eran Yahav
papers.standfirst: A programming language for reasoning about transformer computation.
intro: The example comments below focus on what a programming perspective could make possible. A highlight can stay this concise when the recommendations already convey why readers are enthusiastic.

endorsements.name: Example reader A
endorsements.text: This changes the kind of questions I want to ask about a model. A small program gives me something concrete to reason about, and I find that a compelling starting point for new work.

endorsements.name: Example reader B
endorsements.text: I like the prospect of using this vocabulary to talk across theory and interpretability. It gives a conversation somewhere precise to begin.
